name: Toothbrush moustache

lead: The toothbrush moustache is a short, trimmed moustache about as wide as the nose, covering the area under the nostrils. Its neat, uniform shape made it popular in the US in the late 1800s and it spread to Germany in the early 1900s.

It rose with figures such as Charlie Chaplin and Oliver Hardy, then largely fell out of favour after World War II because of its association with Adolf Hitler. Today it is still widely read as evoking him.

paras: People who wear it keep the moustache clipped short and tidy, so it reads as a small, compact rectangle. Its low-maintenance appeal was part of its early popularity.
The main consideration is social perception: the style remains linked to Hitler in many countries, though it is legal in Germany.

chain: Frames the mouth with a compact, tidy line
angle.text: It adds a small, defined line of hair above the lip and requires little upkeep. People choose it as a deliberate retro or character look.

lead: The toothbrush moustache is a facial hair style: a small, neat rectangle of hair on the upper lip. It became popular in the United States in the late 1800s, where its tidy, uniform look suited the era of industrial standardisation and contrasted with imperial, walrus and handlebar styles.[1]

It spread to Germany through American visitors, and by 1907 The New York Times reported German men wearing it. By the end of World War I some German royals, including Crown Prince Wilhelm, wore it.[1]

Charlie Chaplin wore it as the Tramp from 1914, and Oliver Hardy wore it from at least 1921. Hitler is generally thought to have adopted it in the early 1920s; after World War II the style fell out of fashion, though a few public figures kept it.[1]
infobox: Charlie Chaplin, Oliver Hardy, Adolf Hitler

paras: Popular in the US from the late 1800s, it reached Germany by 1907 and gained prominence after Hans Koeppen's 1908 New York to Paris race.[1] Chaplin added it to the Tramp in 1914 to look older, and his 1940 film The Great Dictator was his last appearance with it.[1]

Wearers have included Charles de Gaulle, Michael Collins, Georgy Zhukov, Francisco Franco, Heinrich Himmler and Robert Mugabe, who wore a philtrum-only version from 1976 to 2016.[1] In the US, 1930s officials such as James Rolph and Frank L. Shaw wore it, as did Fred Trump.[1]

After World War II the association with Hitler made it unfashionable. In 1923 Ernst Hanfstaengl reportedly urged Hitler to drop it, and he replied that it would become fashionable because he wore it.[1] It remains legal in Germany despite that country's ban on Nazi symbols.[1]
